title: Common Nodics Implementation Examples
readerIntent: Choose the correct Nodics ownership and extension pattern for common changes.
priorKnowledge: Read application capability, API, customization, testing, and documentation guides.
summary: Use these decision examples to place common changes in their existing authority instead of creating parallel implementations.

sections.heading: Example: add a governed business field
items: Define the business meaning, owner, data type, required and immutable behavior, visibility, write permissions, tenant scope, import/export representation, search need, and migration before editing a schema.
Add the field through the customer project's layered schema contribution and reuse generated item and search models. Put policy names in properties.js so another layer can customize them.
Exercise create, read, update, search, field masking, invalid input, unauthorized groups, legacy records, import, export, indexing, cache, API contract, and rollback.
Update the functional guide with a business example and the developer guide with configuration, extension, migration, testing, operations, and limitations.

sections.heading: Example: add an external provider
items: Implement the provider-specific adapter behind the existing database, cache, search, event, or AI gateway and register capabilities without adding vendor branches to callers.

Configuration declares activation, connection secret references, limits, timeouts, retries, circuits, fallback, and provider-specific options; only one authoritative selection path resolves the active adapter.
Test normalized success, mapping, timeout, cancellation, partial failure, retry safety, outage, recovery, telemetry, security, compatibility, load, and cost where applicable.
Document local setup separately from production qualification and never commit machine paths, credentials, or insecure development switches.

sections.heading: Examples
items: Add a field: extend the owning schema in a later project module, regenerate derived models/contracts, migrate or import data safely, and test old/new records.
Change a runtime value: expose it in properties.js and, only when operational updates are required, use the existing governed runtime configuration contract with validation, audit, and rollback.
Add an API: define an owned route, thin controller, facade orchestration, service behavior, schema model access, permissions, status codes, OpenAPI, and boundary tests.
Add a scheduled action: use CronJob with module/service identity; never reuse human username/password credentials.
Add a business approval: use Workflow actions that may be manual or automatic; do not turn a technical pipeline into a durable business process.
Integrate a provider: implement the existing provider-neutral adapter and selection configuration; callers must not reference the vendor directly.
Build a web UI: keep presentation/renderers in the client repository, load governed content and contracts, and call owning backend modules rather than placing business logic in the browser.

sections.heading: Review checklist
items: Existing authority searched and reused where possible.
Owner, contract, configuration, security, observability, failure/retry, performance, deployment, and rollback are explicit.
No duplicate loader, registry, persistence, workflow, API, or documentation authority exists.
Positive, negative, boundary, contract, integration, resilience, and regression evidence is present.
Canonical documentation and concise module README match the code.

sections.heading: Complete guide: Common Implementation Examples
paragraphs: This guide explains how to implement common Nodics changes without guessing where code belongs.
Use it when you need to create an API, create or change a schema, add a provider implementation, create a scheduled job, or change runtime configuration.
The same rule applies to every example:

```text
Capabilities are sacred; implementations are negotiable.
```

That means the capability contract must stay stable, while the implementation can come from framework modules, project modules, provider modules, environment modules, server modules, node modules, tenant configuration, or runtime governance.

sections.heading: How To Use These Examples
paragraphs: Each example follows the same beginner-friendly pattern:
If an AI tool is helping, ask it to explain these ten points before it writes code. That makes the implementation easier to review and prevents new behavior from landing in a random helper file.
items: Identify the business or platform capability.
Choose the owning module or later project layer.
Put each part of the change in the correct Nodics layer.
Keep configuration in `config/properties.js`.
Keep behavior in `src/service`.
Keep API request mapping in `src/controller`.
Keep orchestration in `src/facade`.
Keep route metadata in `src/router/routers.js`.
Keep data definitions in `src/schemas/schemas.js`.
Add tests and regenerate generated artifacts.

sections.heading: Quick Placement Map
paragraphs:
| Change | Main files |
| --- | --- |
| New API | `src/router/routers.js`, `src/controller`, `src/facade`, `src/service`, tests |
| New data model | `src/schemas/schemas.js`, `src/search/indexes.js` if searchable, tests |
| New provider | Provider module `config/properties.js`, `src/service`, DAO/adapter files, tests |
| New scheduled job | CronJob data/config, job service, optional pipeline/event hooks, tests |
| New import rule | Import pipeline, interceptor, service, config, tests |
| New cache behavior | Cache properties, route/schema/service cache metadata, invalidation tests |
| New tenant-specific behavior | Tenant/runtime configuration plus tenant-aware service tests |
| New documentation route or API contract behavior | Router metadata, OpenAPI generation, Swagger/docs tests |

sections.heading: Before You Start
paragraphs: Describe the requirement in one sentence:

```text
This change allows <user or system> to <do something> so that <business outcome>.
```
Then answer:
Do not write code until the owner and layer are clear.
items: Which module owns this capability?
Is this framework behavior or project-specific behavior?
Is the change tenant-specific, environment-specific, server-specific, or node-specific?
Is this source behavior, generated behavior, configuration, data, documentation, or tests?
Which extension point lets a project change this later without editing framework files?

sections.heading: Example Review Questions
paragraphs: Before accepting a change from a human developer or AI tool, ask:
items: Did it name the owning module?
Did it avoid changing framework code for project-specific behavior?
Did it use standard folders and `module.exports`?
Did it keep permissions visible in route metadata?
Did it keep tenant-sensitive behavior tenant-aware?
Did it update generated artifacts when schemas or routes changed?
Did it include tests for success, failure, permission, tenant, and override behavior where relevant?
Did it update public docs, module README, and LLM context when behavior changed?

sections.heading: Common Verification Checklist
paragraphs: Before committing a functional change, run the smallest relevant test first and then the governance checks required by the change:

```bash
npm run ai:validate
npm run ai:principle-audit
npm run llm:generate
npm run llm:validate
npm run quality:docs
```

Use broader suites such as `npm run test:basic`, `npm run test:full`, or release-grade integration gates when the change affects shared framework behavior, topology, external providers, generated artifacts, security, tenant isolation, or runtime governance.

sections.heading: What To Avoid
paragraphs: Avoid:
items: changing framework files for customer-specific behavior;
creating custom folders that Nodics loaders cannot see;
hardcoding permissions, provider choices, endpoints, credentials, schedules, or policy values;
bypassing services, facades, pipelines, interceptors, or runtime governance;
editing generated artifacts manually;
adding behavior without tests;
updating public behavior without updating documentation and generated LLM context.
